C A U T E R Y.

<margin>15.</margin>
Therefore, pus is blood corrupted in the part where the wound is, and it is the effect of a digestion corrupted in that same place. To have corrupted the integrity, continuity, and digestion of the parts, and finally to have converted the blood into pus, is what has been deemed in the *Schools* to be an encounter with <term>Catarrhs</term> <gloss>pathological discharges of rheum</gloss>: whether it be that they have extracted through the hole of a cautery an excremental humor (which otherwise had threatened to settle upon a noble part) from the head (whence they all originally seek the source of *Catarrhs*): or whether there is meanwhile a consensus between the head and the wounded part, or not; for it is the same thing, provided the wounded skin is kept open. Whether that excremental humor be blood, or becomes pus, or sanies <note>a thin, unhealthy discharge from a wound</note>, it is all the same, provided the world is deceived by the worn-out terms of Catarrh, precaution, derivation, revulsion, and the <term>fontanelle</term> <gloss>a small artificial ulcer used for drainage</gloss>. For I observe an infant of a year old, already teething, and suffering from a fever, foam of the mouth, and incessant saliva. And finally, there are torments <note>colic or bowel pains</note>, and stools that are yellow-green. Yet that tooth is a part of the head; therefore, the diarrhea will be a Catarrh of the head. But what is the consensus of an erupting tooth, or of a swollen gum, with the intestine? Or what is its power to generate and send a Catarrh from the stomach of an infant to the head, and thence into the <term>Ileon</term> <gloss>the third portion of the small intestine</gloss>? By what right will a vapor distilled from the stomach become greenish bile in the head? Has the workshop of bile perhaps migrated to the head since the beginning of life? Could a cautery (if the infant were able to endure it) drive away a leek-green diarrhea into itself? And compensate for several pounds of leek-green bile with a few little drops of pus? Why does the infant's stomach manufacture a Catarrh on account of a toothache? Why is it sent into the intestine, and not to the aching tooth? Does the reader not yet see that diarrhea is not a Catarrh? But rather that the indignant <term>Archeus</term> <gloss>the vital internal principle or spirit</gloss>, being present anywhere in the intestine, is ready to transmute the alimentary chyme into excrements, which are thought by the *Schools* to be bile, phlegm, etc. If, therefore, diarrhea is not a Catarrh, and the indignant <term>Archeus</term> can transmute anything into an offensive liquid, provided the gum is afflicted, will it not be able to discharge itself in any direction through the established drainage channels? And not wait for the skin to be opened by a caustic agent? Ah, what cruel dullness has caused the *Schools* to rage against mortals who are their own kin?

<column-break/>

<margin>16.</margin>
For they do not consider that in women, and in the obese, there is a fleshy membrane around the ordinary places for a cautery, which is pure fat to the thickness of at least two fingers, to whom, however, more frequent and supposedly more beneficial cauteries are recommended. Wherefore, the bottom of the <term>fontanelle</term> <gloss>draining ulcer</gloss> will hardly be in the middle of the fat. 
<margin>17.</margin>
There is therefore no path through which an evil, fictitious humor, proscribed as a *Catarrh*, might rush from the brain, or between the skull and the skin, through the substance of the fat. But what, finally, is that solitary humor which, having been proscribed by the sending part for its own fault, descends unmixed through the substance of the fat and degenerates into pus? If it is an exhalation of vapors from the stomach, why will it not be more frequent in the young and those with warm stomachs, than in the weak, the old, and the cold? By what means will this water, distilled from vapor, take on the form of pus? How will it hasten through the brain, the meninges, and the skull to find the hole made by a cautery, so that it may flow out and be purged only there? Why does the vapor not fly off into the air a hundred times before it reaches the place designed by the eager cautery? How will water ascending from the stomach suddenly be blood, and the matter of pus? How will blood (the matter of pus, according to *Galen*) be the matter of a *Catarrh*? Why must blood be reduced to the series of evil humors, when it is not yet contaminated, and is dispensed by nature to the wounded place? Why, once a wound is made, will nature cease to expel the damned matter through and into the places customary to it? For will she, upon the skin being opened at the surgeon's pleasure, become ignorant of her devious paths? Or perhaps she has labored only to find an exit somewhere? And that having been done, will she henceforth come to obey the one who inflicts the wound? Thus, these four things are false, namely,

<summary>Van Helmont critiques the medical theory of "catarrhs" and the use of cauteries (fontanelles) for drainage, arguing that these practices are based on a misunderstanding of how the body's vital principle, the Archeus, manages illness and waste.</summary>
<keywords>cautery, catarrh, Archeus, medicine, fontanelle, digestion, humor theory</keywords>
